ray-elements and raylang

ray-elements is framework-agnostic: the components are standard custom elements with no dependencies, and they work in any page, in React, in Vue, in a browser or in any webview. Nothing in a component requires raylang.

raylang is where ray-elements comes from and where it gets extras. This page says what those extras are: a bridge to the native side (plan 1), and a raylang package that brings the whole design system without npm (plan 2).

Today

  • Tooling in raylang. Tokens, contrast checks, docs, the npm packages and the browser tests are generated and run by tools/ (tools/run.sh build).
  • Made for the std/ui webview. No build step: the elements load as ES modules from ray://app, and form fields are form-associated, so a FormData reaches the program through window.ray.send or window.ray.request as it is.
  • Examples. examples/desktop-form (plain HTML), examples/react-app and examples/vue-app (made with ray new --frontend react-ts|vue-ts) drive the page in the real webview and check what reaches raylang.
  • The raylang package (plan 2): the elements dependency brings @raylang/elements to the app's pages by its npm name (import "@raylang/elements/button", as with a bundler), with no npm and no copied files; examples/starter is the app to copy. It is published to its own repository, github.com/ray-language/elements.
  • The native bridge (plan 1, done): system file dialogs with real paths (ray-file-upload native, ray-path-input), native confirmations (confirmDialog()), native context menus (ray-menu native), the app's menu bar in the command palette (native-menus), and the window: ray-app-shell under a transparent title bar, window colors that follow the theme, and the "unsaved changes" mark (trackEdits). See below, the "In a raylang app" section of each component's page, and examples/desktop-app.

Using the bridge

In the program, answer the bridge before the app's own events (elements = "path:…/ray-elements/elements" in [dependencies] inside this repository; an app elsewhere uses git+https://github.com/ray-language/elements@v0.3.0 once that version is tagged):

import std/ui;
import elements/bridge;

for e in ui.events() {
    if (bridge.handle(e)) {
        continue;   // a ray-elements request, already answered
    }
    // the app's own events
}

In the page, once:

import { enableRaylang } from "@raylang/elements/core";   // or from "@raylang/elements"
await enableRaylang();   // the host, or null in a browser
<ray-file-upload native multiple accept=".png,.jpg" label="Photos"></ray-file-upload>
<ray-path-input name="out" label="Export to" mode="save" accept=".csv"></ray-path-input>

ray-file-upload native lists the chosen files as HostFiles (name, size, type and path), gives their paths in paths and submits the paths with its form; drop and paste still give Files. ray-path-input shows Browse… only with the host. confirmDialog() asks with the system dialog unless native: false. In a browser all of them behave as before.

For menus, keep one Native for the whole loop, declare the menus through it and use route(), which turns an item run from the palette into the same "menu" event the menu bar sends:

let n = bridge.system();
bridge.menu(n, "File", [ui.item("new", "New", "cmd+n"), ui.item("open", "Open…", "cmd+o")])?;
for raw in ui.events() {
    let e = match (bridge.route(n, raw)) {
        Option.Some(e) => e,      // for the app
        Option.None => continue,  // answered by the bridge
    };
    if (e.kind == "menu") { … }   // from the menu bar or from the palette
}
<ray-command-palette native-menus></ray-command-palette>
<ray-menu native context>
  <div slot="trigger">…</div>
  <ray-menu-item value="rename">Rename</ray-menu-item>
</ray-menu>

bridge.menu_at, replace_menu and set_menu_item keep the record up to date the same way (bridge.record records a menu without touching the bar).

The window: open it with o.kind = "full_content" and enableRaylang() sets --ray-titlebar-height and --ray-titlebar-inset (the room for the macOS window buttons) on <html>; a ray-app-shell then makes its header the title bar (taller, indented, dragging the window) or, with layout="alt" or no header, starts its navbar and main below it. dragRegion(el) does the same for any element of your own. enableRaylang() also keeps the window's background and title bar in the theme's background color (windowColors: false to opt out), and trackEdits(form) marks the window as edited while the form differs from what was saved:

import { enableRaylang, trackEdits } from "@raylang/elements";
await enableRaylang();
const edits = trackEdits(document.querySelector("form"));   // edits.dirty, edits.clean()

Principles

  • The components stay agnostic. No component imports the bridge. Without it, every component behaves exactly as it does today, in any host.
  • Opt-in and detectable. The bridge is one module, enabled by the app, and only active when window.ray exists. A page shared between a browser and a std/ui window works in both.
  • One source of truth. The package, its assets and its types are generated by the same build that writes the npm packages, from the same component.toml files.

Plan 1: the native bridge

A small protocol between the page and the program, with two halves:

  • Page: core/raylang.js (in @raylang/elements, also re-exported from its index). enableRaylang() detects window.ray, asks the program for its capabilities once ("hello") and installs a host in core/host.js, the registry the components ask; they never import the bridge.
  • Program: a raylang module, elements/bridge (the elements/ directory of this repo), with one entry point for the app's event loop:
import std/ui;
import elements/bridge;

for e in ui.events() {
    if (bridge.handle(e)) {
        continue;   // a ray-elements request, already answered
    }
    // the app's own events
}

Requests travel through window.ray.request as JSON ({"ray-elements": 1, "op": "pick_files", …}) and bridge.handle answers them with ui.reply_json: {"ok": true, "value": …} or {"ok": false, "error": "…"}. Anything else passes through untouched, so the bridge coexists with the app's own protocol. The dialogs sit behind a Native struct (bridge.system()); handle_with(e, n) takes another one, which is how the webview tests answer with scripted dialogs.

Operation Asks for Answers
hello {protocol, version, platform, ops}
pick_files title, directory, multiple, filters [{path, name, size}], [] if cancelled
pick_path mode (open, folder, save), title, directory, suggested, filters the path, or null
confirm title, message, confirmLabel, cancelLabel, style true / false
menu_items [{menu, tag, title, shortcut, enabled, checked}] (no separators, no role:*)
run_menu tag true; route() gives the app the "menu" event
popup_menu id, items (title, enabled, checked, separator) true once shown; the choice comes later as the page event ray-elements:menu ({id, index}), nothing when dismissed
window_colors background, titlebar (#rrggbb, "" = system) true
set_edited edited true

What the components get

Component With the bridge raylang API
ray-file-upload "browse" opens the native dialog with filters built from accept and returns real paths (paths property, read on change); drop and paste keep working with File objects ui.pick_files, ui.file_options, ui.filter
ray-path-input (new) a field with a "Browse…" button for a file, a folder or a save target, showing the chosen path; without the bridge it is a plain text field ui.pick_file_with, ui.pick_folder_with, ui.save_file_with
ray-command-palette lists the app's native menu items next to its own commands, with their shortcuts; running one emits the same menu event as the menu ui.menu (recorded through bridge.menu)
ray-menu native attribute: opens as a native context menu at the pointer; the choice arrives as ray-select ui.popup_menu
confirmDialog() asks with the native, modal dialog instead of a ray-dialog ui.confirm, ui.message_styled
ray-sidebar, app header in a full_content window, reserve window.ray.titlebar_height and mark the header as the drag handle (data-ray-drag), so the page runs under a transparent macOS title bar window kind full_content
Theme when the user picks light, dark or a primary color, the window background and title bar follow, so a resize or reopen never flashes the other theme ui.set_background, ui.set_titlebar_color
Forms optional edited tracking: a dirty form marks the window as edited (the macOS dot) ui.set_edited
Attachments "open" and "show in folder" for an attachment with a path ui.open_path, ui.reveal

Milestones

  1. ✅ Protocol and loop. core/raylang.js and elements/bridge with capability negotiation, pick_files and confirm. Tests: the raylang tests of bridge.answer, and tests/bridge.test.js, where the page talks to the real bridge in the webview runner (scripted dialogs).
  2. ✅ Files. ray-file-upload native and the new ray-path-input (pick_path), with their React/Vue wrappers and types.
  3. ✅ Menus. bridge.menu (and menu_at, replace_menu, set_menu_item), route(), the palette listing native items (native-menus), ray-menu native.
  4. ✅ Window. full_content support in ray-app-shell (header as the title bar, dragRegion), theme to window colors, trackEdits. The drag handle worked around finding #138 (the shell's data-ray-drag did not see shadow DOM; fixed in raylang 1.27.48); it still spares the interactive elements the shell does not know, such as tabs and summary.
  5. ✅ Docs and example. An "In a raylang app" section on the pages of file upload, path input, dialog, menu, command palette and app shell (from each component's raylang.md), and examples/desktop-app, which uses all of it: ray run src/main.ray --check drives it in a real full_content window with scripted dialogs (the system's dialogs and menus cannot be clicked by a script; try them with ray run).

Each milestone ships on its own and keeps the components working without the bridge.

Plan 2: the raylang package

The elements/ directory of this repo is a raylang package: a raylang app gets the whole design system from it, with no npm, no Node and no copied files.

[dependencies]
elements = "git+https://github.com/ray-language/elements@v0.3.0"
# or, next to a checkout of this repository: elements = "path:../ray-elements/elements"
import std/ui;
import elements/bridge;

fn main() -> int {
    ui.mount_embed_at("", "assets").unwrap();   // the app's page ([native] embed)
    let h = ui.open("App", "ray://app/index.html", 960, 640).unwrap();
    for e in ui.events() {
        if (bridge.handle(e)) {
            continue;
        }
        // the app's own events
    }
    0
}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/node_modules/@raylang/elements/tokens.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/node_modules/@raylang/elements/base.css">
<script type="module">
  import { enableRaylang } from "@raylang/elements";   // every component, and the API
  await enableRaylang();
</script>

The page imports @raylang/elements by its npm name, the same as an app built with Vite: import "@raylang/elements/button", import { enableRaylang } from "@raylang/elements/core". The package's ray.toml declares it ([web] package = "web"), and raylang (the package needs 1.27.48 or later) does the rest, under ray run and in a native binary:

  • it serves the package at ray://app/node_modules/@raylang/elements/, where npm would put it (so the stylesheets are linked by that path);
  • it injects an import map built from the package's exports into every HTML page of ray://app/ (ui.import_map() returns it; a page with its own import map is left as is);
  • ray run and ray fetch link the package into the app's node_modules/@raylang/elements, so the editor resolves the same imports with their types (ray-elements.d.ts) and goes to their definitions. Add node_modules/ to the app's .gitignore. Three small files make every editor see everything, the same as in a Vite project (examples/lean-app has them): a package.json that declares "dependencies": { "@raylang/elements": "*" } (the Deno language server only resolves a package the project declares), a tsconfig.json with "allowJs": true, "moduleResolution": "bundler" and the dom lib (read by TypeScript and by Deno), and .vscode/settings.json with "html.customData": ["./node_modules/@raylang/elements/vscode.html-custom-data.json"] for the <ray-*> tags and their attributes.

examples/starter is that app, ready to copy (ray new --frontend takes npm create vite templates, so it cannot start one without npm). examples/desktop-app uses the package and the whole bridge.

Contents

  • elements/web (generated by build): a copy of packages/elements, the npm package @raylang/elements as it is published — index.js (every component, and the API: enableRaylang, notify, confirmDialog…), core.js, core/, components/, tokens.css, base.css, the types and the editor data. A page that uses a few components imports @raylang/elements/<name> instead of @raylang/elements, and @raylang/elements/core for the API alone (enableRaylang, setIcons…). examples/lean-app does it, and loads its settings dialog with import() on first open; its --check fails if the page defines any other element.
  • elements/version (generated): version.VERSION, the version of ray-elements.toml; the bridge's hello answers with it. The other modules import it as elements/version, the only form that also works from an app (finding #142).
  • elements/bridge (plan 1, hand-written).
  • elements/README.md (hand-written), LICENSE and NOTICE (copies of the repository's): the package is the whole directory. build keeps the version of ray.toml and of the README's install line.
  • No mod.ray: it would make the other modules internal to the capsule, so the package is import elements/bridge; (and elements/version).

How the assets travel: decided by the spike

The package must work under ray run, in a native binary and in a bundle, where the app runs from any directory and only what was baked in exists.

  1. The package embeds them (its own [native] embed): does not work. A dependency's embed is ignored, under ray run and in a native binary: std/embed only has the app's own files, also when the package reads it (finding #139).
  2. Generated module (chosen until 0.3.0): build wrote the 86 files (about 690 KB of source) as string constants of elements/assets.ray, and assets.mount("ray-elements") served them at ray://app/ray-elements/…. It worked under ray run and in a native binary, but the pages imported ./ray-elements/components/button/button.js: a path that only existed in the window, that the editor could not resolve, and that looked nothing like the npm names.
  3. The npm package, served by raylang (chosen): raylang 1.27.43 made a dependency's [native] embed reach the app (#139), and 1.27.44 added [web] package, which serves a dependency's npm package by its npm name, with an import map, and links it into the app's node_modules/ for the editor. elements/web is now packages/elements as published; the generated module is gone, and the pages read the same as with a bundler. examples/lean-app, examples/starter and examples/desktop-app pass their --check under ray run, and examples/lean-app also as a native binary run from another directory.

Milestones

  1. ✅ Spike on the two asset routes: the generated module.
  2. ✅ Package in elements/, generated by build, with mount and a raylang test that checks every file.
  3. ✅ Starter example and its --check.
  4. ✅ Publish (both repositories are public; the first index entry comes with the v0.3.0 tag). What the spike found about dependencies decided how:
    • a git+ dependency puts the root of the repository in .ray-deps/<key> and imports it by the key; there is no way to point at a subdirectory (finding #140), and the packages of the index are one repository each, with the modules at the root (greeting, for instance). So elements/ cannot be installed from this repository as it is: git+https://github.com/ray-language/ray-elements would give the docs site's repository, not the package.
    • So the package has a repository of its own, ray-language/elements, published like the packages of the raylang monorepo: ray registry mirror (raylang 1.27.43), run from elements/ on a maintainer's machine at each tag, snapshots the directory into that repository, tags it and adds the version to the index. No deploy key and no CI secret. An app installs it with ray add elements (the index) or pins the tag with git+https://github.com/ray-language/elements@v0.3.0 (checked with a copy of examples/starter outside this repository).
  5. ✅ By the npm name: the package carries @raylang/elements as published ([web] package, raylang 1.27.44); the pages import it as with a bundler and the editor resolves it from node_modules/.

Later ideas

  • Typed HTML from raylang. From the same component.toml, generate a raylang module for compiled .ray.html templates with typed attributes (variant as an enum), so a misspelled variant fails at compile time. Since raylang 1.27.39 the compiled templates are documented and report clear errors (findings #126, #127 and #131 are resolved), so this no longer waits on raylang; it is the next candidate after plans 1 and 2.
  • Tokens in raylang. A generated tokens.ray, so charts drawn by the program, icons, the Info.plist colors or a native shell use the same palette as the UI.
  • UI tests for apps. The webview harness of tools/ as a utility: an app that uses ray-elements drives its own pages in the real webview from ray test.
  • System notifications. ray-notification could fall back to an OS notification when the window is not focused, but std/ui has no notification API today.
